item.title: Emacs | Project.el
item.description:
youtube

,### Install ```emacs-lisp (use-package project :ensure nil :custom (project-vc-extra-root-markers '(".project"))) ``` ,### Project Core Commands * `C-x p f` : `project-find-file` - Search and open a file inside the current project. * `C-x p p` : `project-switch-project` - Switch to another project from your list of known projects. * `C-x p b` : `project-switch-to-buffer` - Switch to an open buffer belonging only to this project. * `C-x p d` : `project-dired` - Open a Dired directory buffer at the root of the project. * `C-x p g` : `project-find-regexp` - Search for a text string or regex across all project files. * `C-x p e` : `project-eshell` - Open a dedicated Eshell terminal instance at the project root. * `C-x p c` : `project-compile` - Run a build or compile command from the project root directory. * `C-x p k` : `project-kill-buffers` - Close all open buffers associated with the current project. ,### Project Management * `M-x project-forget-project` : Remove a specific directory from Emacs' remembered project list. * `M-x project-forget-projects-under` : Remove all saved projects under a specific directory. * `M-x project-forget-zombie-projects` : Automatically remove all non-existent or deleted project directories from the saved list. ,### Other videos on this topic * https://youtu.be/6PlrXQ0tnQM?si=ELMnp_ZpwXSQhMZa * https://www.youtube.com/live/O6hMwJfaXV8?si=lbG6gf4vVatyFQSu

item.title: Full IDE Power Over SSH: Remote C++ Development with Just a Terminal and Emacs
item.description:
youtube

Everything in this video runs over a plain SSH connection to a remote Linux box — no GUI, no forwarded X11, no VS Code Remote extension. Just a terminal, SSH, and Emacs configured as a full C++ IDE. I walk through: • Symbol navigation — jump to definitions across your own code and the C++ standard library, find every reference, and jump back out, all without leaving the keyboard • Refactoring — project-wide rename backed by clangd, not text search-and-replace • Debugging — breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, stepping, live variable inspection, and expression evaluation via DAP (lldb/gdb), fully interactive over a terminal session The point isn't "Emacs is old-school" — it's that terminal + SSH + Emacs is a genuinely fast, lightweight way to work on remote code: no laggy remote-GUI protocol, no heavyweight remote-extension server, works the same whether you're on a fast connection or a rough one. Config used in this video (MIT licensed, free to use/fork): https://github.com/jclosure/vscode-flavored-emacs-2026 ,#emacs #ssh #cpp #remotedevelopment #terminal #linux #debugging #clangd #vscode #dape

item.title: Stop Installing Every Emacs Package You See
item.description:
youtube

How many Emacs packages should a beginner install? In this clip, I ask Protesilaos whether he recommends Denote to someone who is just getting started with Emacs. His answer is simple: start with the basics and only install packages when you understand the problem they are solving. Prot has written many Emacs packages, including the Modus themes, which became part of core Emacs, but he still warns beginners against blindly copying package configurations. When you install tools before understanding your own workflow, you can quickly end up with a bloated Emacs config full of packages you never actually use. We also take a quick look at some of the packages he personally uses, including Denote, TMR, and Substitute, a package for fast search-and-replace operations based on the symbol at point. The main lesson is not that extra Emacs packages are bad. They are useful only when they solve a real need you already have. This clip comes from my second Emacs coaching session with Protesilaos, an Emacs contributor and the creator of packages such as the Modus themes, Denote, and many others, full interview here: https://youtube.com/live/Crp2e5D_Q78 ,#Emacs #VanillaEmacs #Protesilaos #EmacsConfig #Denote #ModusThemes #Linux #TextEditor
